title: Binary: Computers use 0s and 1s.
body: The binary system is the fundamental way computers represent values as 0s and 1s. While humans primarily use the decimal system, computers process data internally based on two states—on and off—similar to electrical signals. Numbers, characters, images, and files are ultimately stored as sequences of 0s and 1s. Even though you won’t deal with binary numbers directly in Python for Beginners, the binary system serves as the foundation for understanding concepts such as bits, bytes, encoding, and file sizes. These cards are not just for memorizing definitions; they serve as supplementary explanations to help you see how these concepts—such as variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows—are connected in actual Python code. Computers represent a great deal of information as combinations of 0s and 1s. Numbers, characters, images, and files are ultimately stored internally as bit patterns. When reading code and encountering binary notation, it’s helpful to remember that the values visible to humans may differ from how the computer stores them. This difference is particularly important when dealing with encoding, files, and network data.
detail: The binary system is the starting point for understanding that the numbers we see may differ from how they are represented internally by a computer. When working with Python’s `bin()` function, integer conversions, file bytes, and encoding, it’s helpful to keep in mind that data is stored as a combination of 0s and 1s. As a beginner, it’s better to focus on the fundamental concept of data representation rather than trying to memorize every bit operation.

title: bit and byte
body: Bits and bytes are the basic units used by computers to store information. A bit represents a single 0 or 1, and a byte is typically a unit consisting of 8 bits. Units such as bytes, KB, and MB frequently appear when reading file sizes, memory usage, and network transfer volumes. In Python, the length of a string may differ from its actual byte size. In particular, characters that use multiple bytes—such as Hangul—must be understood in the context of their encoding. A bit is the smallest unit of information, representing either 0 or 1, while a byte is typically a unit consisting of 8 bits. You’ll frequently encounter these when dealing with file sizes, memory, and encoding. When reading code, data in bytes may be handled differently than strings. body: An integer is a data type that represents numbers without a decimal point. In Python, values such as 1, 2, and 100 correspond to the `int` type. Integers are often used to represent exact values, such as counts, order, indices, and scores. The string '10' and the number 10 may look similar at first glance, but because they are different data types, the results of calculations or comparisons may differ. title: Floating-point error
body: Floating-point error is a small discrepancy that occurs because computers cannot accurately represent decimal values. For example, a number like 0.1 may seem simple to humans, but it may not be stored exactly as intended in a computer’s internal binary representation. As a result, the outcome of decimal calculations may differ very slightly from what is expected. In Python, concepts such as `round`, `Decimal`, and tolerance are important when calculating amounts or performing precise comparisons. Be careful when comparing decimals while reading code. title: Character Encoding and UTF-8
body: Character encoding is the process of converting characters into a set of numerical values that a computer can store. UTF-8 is widely used because it can represent a wide variety of characters, including Hangul, English, and special characters. If the encoding is incorrect when reading a file, the characters may appear garbled. In Python, it is common to specify the encoding, such as `read_text(encoding='utf-8')`. When reading code that handles Korean text files or JSON files, you should also check the encoding settings. title: Type System
body: A type system is a set of rules that defines the types of values. In Python, each value has a data type—for example, 3 is an int, '3' is a str, and [1, 2] is a list. Even if two values appear to be the same—such as 3—they may behave differently in addition or comparison operations if one is a string. Understanding the type system helps you grasp why a value received via `input`—even if it looks like a number—must first be converted to an `int`. When reading code, it’s important to get into the habit of checking the actual data type rather than just what the value appears to be. title: JSON and JSONL
body: JSON and JSONL are formats frequently used for storing and exchanging data. JSON represents object or list structures as strings, while JSONL places a single JSON object on a single line. A single JSON file is sufficient for small configuration files, but JSONL can be more convenient for large training datasets or logs. In Python, you can use `json.loads` to convert a string into a dictionary or list, and `json.dumps` to convert it back into a string. When reading code, you must distinguish whether the entire file is a single JSON object or if each line contains a separate JSON object. title: batch and shard
body: “Batch” and “shard” are terms frequently used when dividing large tasks into smaller parts for processing. A “batch” is a unit consisting of multiple items processed at once, while a “shard” is a large dataset or scope of work divided into multiple pieces. For example, instead of validating 1,000 cards all at once, it is easier to manage them by processing them in batches of 100. When a shard number or batch size appears in the code, you must verify which part of the overall task is being processed and ensure there are no duplicates or omissions. title: mutable / immutable
summary: A mutable value is one whose content can change after it is created, while an immutable value is one whose content does not change after it is created.
